name: 24/7 Emergency Electrician
metaTitle: 24/7 Emergency Electrician in Broward | Ghost Crown
metaDescription: Need a 24/7 emergency electrician in Broward County? Ghost Crown Electric is a Florida Certified, owner led master electrician. We show up day or night.
intro: It is eleven at night and a tenant just called. The air conditioning is dead, half the outlets are out, and the breaker will not stay on. That is the call this company was built around. When power fails after hours you do not need a promise for next week, you need a licensed electrician who picks up and shows up. We show up whenever you call. Day or night. With three trucks on the road we can run three jobs at once, so an emergency at one property does not sit behind another. Electricity is something we do not see, we only feel the effect, and when the effect is a hot night with no cooling we treat it that way. You are paying for the experience, and for someone who actually answers the phone.

definition.heading: What a 24/7 emergency electrician does
definition.body: An emergency electrician handles the electrical failures that cannot wait for a regular appointment: a dead circuit feeding critical equipment, a panel that trips and will not reset, a burning smell, sparking, or a sudden loss of power to part of a building. The work is to find the fault quickly, make the situation safe, and restore power where it is safe to do so. Some problems are an in and out type of situation and are handled on the spot. Others need parts, a utility call, or a permit, and we tell you that honestly before we start. The point of the after-hours visit is real availability at night, not a rushed guess. We diagnose first, then price the fix so you know the number before the work begins.

symptoms.title: Part of the building lost power
symptoms.body: The lights are out in one unit or one wing while the rest of the property still works. When the outage stops at your property line it is not the utility, it is an electrical fault we can locate and repair.

symptoms.title: A breaker will not stay on
symptoms.body: You reset the breaker and it trips again in seconds, or it will not reset at all. That breaker is doing its job and telling you a circuit is overloaded, shorted, or failing. It needs a licensed eye, not a bigger breaker.

symptoms.title: Burning smell or scorch marks
symptoms.body: You notice a hot plastic smell, warm cover plates, or brown scorch marks near an outlet, switch, or the panel. Stop using that circuit and call. This is the kind of sign we take seriously and come out for.

symptoms.title: Outlets or a circuit went dead
symptoms.body: A row of outlets or a whole circuit quit with no warning, and resetting the GFCI and the breaker did nothing. Something upstream has failed. We trace the circuit back to the fault and restore it safely.

symptoms.title: Flickering, dimming, or buzzing
symptoms.body: Lights dim or flicker across the property, or you hear a buzz or crackle at the panel. Those are early warnings of a loose connection or a tired panel. Catching it now beats meeting it at midnight later.

symptoms.title: Critical equipment lost power at night
symptoms.body: The air conditioning, a well pump, a lift station, or another system a tenant depends on lost power after hours. That cannot wait until morning in South Florida heat, and it does not have to. We come out.

process.title: You call and we triage
process.body: The owner takes the call and asks the right questions: what failed, what still works, any smell or spark. That phone triage tells us whether it is safe to wait, safe to reset, or a truck out the door right now.

process.title: On-site assessment
process.body: We arrive and find the actual fault instead of guessing. The $240 service call covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis, so you are paying for a real diagnosis, not a sales visit.

process.title: One forecast-based price
process.body: Once we know what is wrong, you get one honest number for the repair before we touch it. We price it once, price it right. The number does not move mid-job unless we find something new and tell you first.

process.title: Our in-house crew does the work
process.body: The same three-person crew that shows up does the repair, not a subcontractor you never met. We restore power where it is safe, and if a part or a utility step is needed we lay out the plan clearly.

process.title: Permit, inspection, and follow-up
process.body: When the fix requires a permit we pull it, and the owner personally meets the inspector. Then we follow up to confirm the property is stable. We show up when we say we will, start to finish.

benefits.title: Power restored safely
benefits.body: The goal is not just lights back on, it is lights back on safely. We find the real fault and fix that, so the problem does not return the next hot night when the load climbs again.

benefits.title: A licensed electrician who answers
benefits.body: You reach a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor and Broward County Master Electrician, not an answering service. We show up whenever you call. Day or night. That availability is the whole point of an emergency line.

benefits.title: One price that holds
benefits.body: You get one honest number before the repair starts, and it does not creep upward mid-job. For a property manager at eleven at night, a price that holds is as valuable as the speed.

benefits.title: Owner-led accountability
benefits.body: The owner takes the call, prices the job, and stands behind it. Speed without accountability is worthless, and accountability without speed is useless at night. This company sells both, from first call to final inspection.

localSections.heading: Aging housing stock and tired panels
localSections.body: Much of Broward County was wired across the nineteen sixties, seventies, and eighties, and a good share of those panels are still in service. Some are known problem lines that age poorly and lose their grip on breakers over time. When a panel like that has run window units and pool pumps through twenty South Florida summers, the failure rarely announces itself politely. It shows up as a breaker that will not reset, a warm panel cover, or a circuit that dies at the worst hour. Most of our after-hours calls trace back to a service or panel that was already near the end of its life and finally gave out under load. When we come out we read the whole picture, not just the one dead circuit, so we can tell you whether this was a one-time fault or a sign the panel itself is asking to be replaced soon.

localSections.heading: Heat, humidity, and salt air
localSections.body: South Florida is hard on electrical equipment in ways inland systems never see. Air conditioning runs eight or nine months a year, so circuits that feed cooling carry heavy load for long stretches, and heat is what finds a loose or corroded connection. Humidity works into panels and outdoor equipment, and salt air off the coast corrodes lugs, bus bars, and meter equipment faster than most owners expect. Corrosion adds resistance, resistance makes heat, and heat is what turns a slow problem into a sudden one at night. That is why so many emergencies here land in the evening after a long hot day of demand. We factor the climate into every diagnosis, because a repair that ignores heat and salt in this region is a repair that comes back.

localSections.heading: Code and permitting in Broward
localSections.body: Emergency work is still real electrical work, and in Broward County that means it is governed by the same permitting and inspection rules as any other job. Making a property safe at night and pulling the required permit are not in conflict; we do the safe stabilization first, then handle the paperwork the right way. When a repair or replacement needs a permit we pull it under our own license and the owner personally meets the inspector rather than sending a stranger. That matters because an emergency fix that skips the permit can haunt a property manager later at sale, at refinance, or at the next inspection. We keep the record clean so the fast fix does not become tomorrow's problem. Permits pulled and inspections attended are part of how we work, not an upsell.

localSections.heading: What insurance carriers watch
localSections.body: Insurance carriers in South Florida have grown strict about electrical systems, and they pay close attention after a claim. If a fire or water event traces back to electrical failure, the carrier will want to know whether the work was done by a licensed contractor and whether it was permitted and inspected. Unpermitted or handyman electrical repairs can slow a claim or put coverage at risk, which is a costly surprise at the worst possible time. When we handle an emergency we document what failed and what we did, pull permits where they are required, and leave you with a clean licensed trail. For a property manager that paper record is part of protecting the owner, not just the tenant, and it is the kind of thing we handle without being asked twice.

guide.title: The complete guide to emergency electrical service in South Florida

sections.heading: What actually counts as an electrical emergency
sections.body: Not every electrical problem is an emergency, and part of an honest electrician's job is telling you which is which. A true emergency is anything that is unsafe or that leaves people without power they depend on. Burning smells, smoke, sparking, warm or discolored outlets and cover plates, a panel that buzzes or feels hot, and any electrical problem paired with water all belong in the call now category, because those point to arcing or overheating that can start a fire. The second kind of emergency is a loss of critical power: air conditioning in July, a well pump, a lift station, security and life safety systems, or a medical device. In South Florida heat, cooling is not a luxury for a tenant, and a dead AC circuit at night is a legitimate emergency call. On the other end, a single dead outlet, a light that will not turn on, or one tripped GFCI that resets and holds can usually wait for a scheduled visit and save you the after-hours premium. When you call, the owner will ask what failed, what still works, and whether there is any smell or spark, and that triage decides how fast a truck rolls. We would rather talk you through a safe overnight wait than charge you for a run you did not need.

sections.heading: Utility problem or electrical problem, and how to tell
sections.body: Before you pay anyone to come out, it helps to know whether the problem is yours or the power company's, because the answer changes who fixes it. The simplest test is to look past your own walls. If the whole street is dark, if your neighbors lost power too, or if the utility is reporting an outage in the area, that is the utility's line to restore and an electrician cannot bring it back any faster. But if the power stops at your property, if it is one unit, one wing, or one circuit while everyone around you still has lights, that is almost always an electrical problem on your side of the meter, and that is our lane. A few other clues point to your system: power that comes and goes, half the house dark while the other half works which can signal a lost leg of service, breakers that trip and will not reset, or dimming that tracks with a big appliance turning on. When you call we will help you sort this out over the phone so you are not paying for a visit that belongs to the power company. We stay in our lane, and part of staying in it is being honest when a problem is not ours to bill for.

sections.heading: What to do before we arrive
sections.body: There are a few safe steps that protect people and property while a truck is on the way, and a few things you should never do. If you smell burning plastic, see smoke, or notice sparks, stop using that circuit and keep people away from it; if anything is actively smoking or on fire, get everyone out and call the fire department first. If a specific appliance or outlet is the obvious source and you can reach the breaker safely, you can switch that one breaker off to remove power from the problem. Do not stand in water to touch anything electrical, do not keep resetting a breaker that trips right back, and never replace a tripping breaker with a larger one, because that breaker is protecting the wire and a bigger one just lets the wire overheat. Leave the main panel closed unless you are simply flipping a labeled breaker. Grab a flashlight rather than candles, note exactly what failed and when, and if a tenant reported it, get their unit number and a callback. Small details like which outlets are dead and whether anything was running when the power dropped help us find the fault faster once we are on site, which keeps the whole visit shorter and cheaper for you.

sections.heading: What happens during an after-hours visit
sections.body: When we arrive at night the first job is a fast, methodical assessment, not a guess. We confirm what has failed, check the panel and the incoming service, and use meters to trace the dead circuit back toward the fault instead of opening walls at random. The $240 service call covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis, and after hours that call carries a premium because you are paying for real availability at night rather than a slot next week. Once we know what is wrong, you get one honest number for the repair before we begin. Many problems are an in and out type of situation: a failed breaker, a burned connection, a bad device, a loose lug, and those we can often make safe and restore the same visit. Others need a part we have to source, a utility disconnect and reconnect, or a permit and inspection, and when that is the case we stabilize what we safely can, explain the plan, and schedule the rest quickly. Either way we do not leave you guessing about cost or next steps. If the problem is fully resolved on that first visit there is no separate return charge. Everything beyond the diagnosis is quoted per situation, because no two failures are the same and we would rather see it before we price it.

sections.heading: Why after-hours costs more, explained plainly
sections.body: It is fair to ask why an emergency visit costs more than a daytime one, and the honest answer is that you are buying availability. During the day the standard service call is $240, and that covers roughly the first two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis. After hours and on emergencies that same visit carries a premium, and the reason is simple: instead of paying for two hours, you are paying for three, because getting a licensed crew out of bed and to your property at midnight has a real cost. What you are actually buying is not just speed. Speed without accountability is worthless, and a fast electrician who cannot stand behind the work is useless to a property manager at eleven at night. Accountability without speed is just as useless when a tenant has no power. We sell both at once, and the premium reflects that. We will always tell you a premium applies before we roll, so there is no surprise on the invoice. What we will not do is inflate the diagnosis, invent problems, or move the number once it is set. We price it once, price it right, and give a customer more than what they pay for, because the property managers who call us at night are the same ones who call us for the planned work in daylight, and that relationship is worth far more than any single after-hours ticket.

sections.heading: How to choose an emergency electrician you can trust
sections.body: At night, when you are tired and a tenant is upset, it is easy to hand the job to whoever answers first, but a few checks protect you. Start with licensing: you want a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor with statewide authority, and here in Broward a county Master Electrician, because that is the difference between someone who guesses and someone who is accountable to the state for the work. Ask whether the person doing the repair is in-house crew or a subcontractor you will never see again, and whether the company pulls permits and attends inspections or quietly skips them. Skipped permits become your problem later at sale or refinance. Ask how they price after-hours work, and be wary of anyone who will not name a premium up front or who quotes a firm repair price sight unseen; every electrical situation is different and the honest ones see it before they promise it. A good emergency electrician also tells you when a problem is the utility's and not yours, rather than billing you for their outage. Ghost Crown Electric has run for ten years, holds 286 permitted projects on public record, and stays in the top tier of Florida contractors by permit quality, and the owner takes the call, prices the job, and meets the inspector personally. When you call, you are not getting a dispatcher and a stranger, you are getting the person whose license is on the line.

sections.heading: After the emergency: making the fix permanent
sections.body: Getting the power back at midnight is the first job, but a good emergency electrician is already thinking about the next hot night. Once the immediate danger is handled, we tell you plainly whether what failed was a one-time fault or a symptom of something larger, like a panel that is losing its grip on breakers or service equipment that is worn out. That honesty lets a property manager plan the permanent repair on their own schedule and budget, in daylight, instead of meeting the same failure again at the worst hour and at an after-hours premium. We never use the stress of the moment to push a big project; every electrical situation is different, and the real fix gets its own site visit and its own honest price. We also leave you with a record of what we found and what we did, which matters when the same issue later touches a tenant complaint or an insurance question. For a building that keeps having small electrical emergencies, that pattern is itself the message: the service is tired and asking for attention. Catching that early, and acting on it when it is convenient rather than when it is smoking, is how you turn a string of midnight calls into one planned, permitted job. That is the whole difference between chasing symptoms and fixing the cause, and it is the reason property managers keep our number in their phone rather than searching for a stranger the next time the lights go out.

faqs.answer: The standard service call is $240 and covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis. After-hours and emergency visits carry a premium over that because you are paying for real availability at night. The repair itself is quoted per situation once we see the fault, and if the problem is resolved on the spot there is no separate return charge.

faqs.question: How is this different from a normal service call?
faqs.answer: A normal service call is a scheduled daytime visit. An emergency visit is the same licensed diagnosis, but after hours and with a premium, because we are getting a crew to you at night. With three trucks we can run three jobs at once, so an emergency at one property does not have to wait behind another job on the calendar.

faqs.question: Is my outage a power company problem or an electrician problem?
faqs.answer: If the whole neighborhood is dark, that is the utility and we cannot restore it faster. If the power stops at your property, or it is one unit or one circuit while your neighbors have lights, that is almost always on your side of the meter and it is our lane. Call us and we will help you tell the difference before anyone comes out.

faqs.question: Can you get the power back on the same night?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Many failures are an in and out type of situation, such as a failed breaker or a burned connection, and we can make them safe and restore power on the first visit. Some problems need a part, a utility disconnect, or a permit, and when that happens we stabilize what is safe and lay out a clear plan for the rest.

faqs.question: Should I keep resetting the breaker while I wait?
faqs.answer: No. A breaker that trips right back is protecting the wire from overheating, and forcing it on repeatedly is not safe. Never swap in a larger breaker either, because that removes the protection. If one labeled breaker is clearly the source, you can leave it off. Otherwise leave the panel alone, keep people clear, and let us find the fault.
